title: Spectral-Domain Deep Learning of Intrinsic Scattering Operators for Arbitrarily Shaped Compact 3D Particles
authors: Daize Li, Jiafu Shen, Yifei Liu, Bonan Zhang, Heping Xie
abstract: Rapid prediction of optical scattering from arbitrarily shaped three-dimensional particles is important for particle optics and photonic characterization, but remains challenging because of the large variability of complex morphologies and the strong angular dependence of their scattering responses. To address both issues, a dual spectral-domain neural scattering model is introduced in which morphology and scattering are represented in physically ordered bases: particle geometry is compressed into only 256 spherical-harmonic coefficients, and the optical response is encoded by the complex T-matrix in a spherical-vector-wave basis. The morphology spectrum replaces high-dimensional Euclidean geometry representations, such as voxel grids, point clouds, or meshes, with a compact ordered descriptor, while the T-matrix represents a geometry-determined scattering operator that can be queried for different incidence directions, polarizations, and observation angles. A spectral-token Transformer trained on 50{,}000 irregular particles at 1064~nm maps the morphology spectrum directly to the T-matrix. The predicted operators recover modal structure and reproduce full-angle differential scattering maps and incidence-angle scans. Generalization to out-of-distribution synthetic shapes and natural sand-particle morphologies shows that the dual spectral architecture learns an intrinsic relation from the geometry spectrum to multipolar scattering. This establishes spectral-domain operator learning as a compact route for reusable, angle- and polarization-resolved optical scattering prediction of complex 3D particles.
summary: This paper introduces a novel dual spectral-domain neural network that predicts the optical scattering T-matrix for complex 3D particles. By encoding particle shape into spherical-harmonic coefficients and using a Transformer, it bypasses computationally intensive electromagnetic solves. This establishes an efficient, data-driven method for reusable, angle-resolved characterization of photonic materials.
main_problem: The challenge is rapidly predicting optical scattering from arbitrarily shaped, complex 3D particles due to morphological variability and strong angular dependence of the response.
main_result: A dual spectral-domain architecture successfully learns an intrinsic relationship mapping a compact geometry spectrum directly to the full T-matrix operator, enabling reusable, angle-resolved prediction.
method: The authors employ a spectral-token Transformer trained on 50,000 particles to map spherical-harmonic coefficients (morphology) to the complex T-matrix (scattering operator).
model_or_system: The system involves electromagnetic scattering from compact irregular particles. The model uses a dual spectral representation: geometry is compressed into an ordered spectrum of spherical-harmonic coefficients, and the response is encoded by the T-matrix in a spherical-vector-wave basis.
key_observables: Full-angle differential scattering maps, incidence-angle scans, and the complex T-matrix itself.
important_parameters: Wavelength (1064 nm), number of SH coefficients (e.g., 256), and generalization performance metrics like $R^2$ ($\approx 0.97$).
main_assumptions: The geometry can be sufficiently represented by a truncated spherical-harmonic spectrum, and the scattering physics can be captured by learning the T-matrix operator directly.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the workflow from morphology encoding to T-matrix computation; one figure shows the Transformer architecture mapping spectral tokens to $	ext{Re}(\mathbf{T})$ and $	ext{Im}(\mathbf{T})$; another validates full-angle scattering maps across incidence scans.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the dual spectral model, details the training process using a spectral-token Transformer on ground-truth T-matrices derived from boundary element methods, demonstrates prediction accuracy for various angles/polarizations, and tests generalization to out-of-distribution shapes.
why_interesting: While focused on classical optics, the methodology of representing complex physical inputs (geometry) and outputs (operator) in highly structured, compact spectral bases suitable for deep learning is analogous to techniques used in quantum state representation or Hamiltonian parameterization.

FIG. 2. Spectral-token Transformer for morphology-to-operator learning. Ordered spherical-harmonic coefficients are grouped into spectral tokens, processed by self-attention layers, aggregated into a latent representation, and decoded into the real and imaginary parts of the finite-order complex T-matrix.

FIG. 3. Learning the intrinsic T-matrix from spectral shape tokens. (a) Training and validation losses. (b) Element-wise agreement between ground-truth and predicted T-matrix entries. (c) Ground-truth and predicted real and imaginary modal maps for one validation particle. (d) Mean relative errors of real and imaginary T-matrix components over the prediction set.

FIG. 4. Physical scattering validation of predicted T-matrices at 1064 nm. Each row shows one irregular particle, full-angle differential scattering maps from the ground-truth and predicted T-matrices, the pointwise relative error, and forward/backward cone integrals during horizontal incidence scans. The same predicted T-matrix is reused throughout the scan.

FIG. 5. Generalization across in-distribution, out-of-distribution synthetic, and real sand-particle morphologies. Box plots show R2 between full-angle differential scattering cross sections computed from reference and predicted T-matrices at 1064 nm for fixed incidence (θi, ϕi) = (90◦, 0◦).
